name: Forehead augmentation (implant or cement)

card.summary: Surgery that builds forehead projection with a custom implant or bone cement, reshaping the upper face for a stronger brow profile.
card.note: Surgical procedure with implant-related risks such as infection or displacement.

quick.overview:
Forehead augmentation adds volume or projection to a flat or receding forehead using a solid implant or a moldable bone cement placed over the frontal bone, usually through a hidden incision.
The appearance payoff described is a more projected, balanced upper face and brow profile, which forum members discuss as part of facial harmony alongside jaw and chin work.
quick.how: Patients commonly choose between a custom-made implant designed from a CT scan and cement applied during surgery. It is done by a craniofacial or plastic surgeon with recovery measured in weeks.
quick.risks: Implant surgeries carry risks including infection, swelling, asymmetry, implant shift and revision. General facial implant sources note that implants are surgically placed devices whose evidence base is mostly clinical series.

lead: Forehead augmentation is a facial contouring operation that increases the projection or smooths the contour of a flat, receding or irregular forehead by adding material over the frontal bone. The two main routes are bone cements (acrylic PMMA or hydroxyapatite) that are shaped by hand during surgery, and solid implants, which are prefabricated or custom-designed from a CT scan [5][1][10]. It belongs to the wider family of facial skeletal implants that also includes chin, cheek and jaw angle implants [2].

People seek it to change the profile and proportions of the upper face. Surgeon-authored descriptions say women who request it generally want a more convex, more vertical forehead, while men more often want a stronger brow bone with a slope that angles back toward the hairline [1]. In looksmaxxing communities it appears in threads about facial implants, implant materials, infection concerns and custom implant designers, usually discussed together with jaw and chin surgery as part of overall facial harmony [3].

The published literature specific to aesthetic forehead augmentation is small and mostly consists of surgeon case descriptions and case series. Broader reviews of facial implant materials and of hydroxyapatite in facial surgery conclude that no material has been shown to be superior and that long-term comparative data are limited [4][5]. Related, better-documented forehead surgery exists in facial feminization, where the forehead is usually reduced or recontoured rather than built up [6][7].

angle.text: The procedure builds forehead contour directly using an implant or cement. People choose it to change the profile and proportions of the upper face, whether to add a gentle convexity or a firmer brow line.

paras: Facial implants are surgically inserted devices that modify facial features for cosmetic or medical reasons; the commonly described family includes chin, cheek, jaw angle and paranasal implants [2]. Forehead procedures follow the same principle but sit over the frontal bone, so the implant or cement must be fitted to a curved surface and blended into the brow and temple areas.

One plastic surgeon who writes extensively on the topic describes forehead augmentation as the most common forehead procedure, typically performed for a flat or recessed forehead, and notes that the desired result differs by sex: a rounder, more vertical forehead for women and a stronger brow with a backward-sloping upper forehead for men [1]. Questions posted to the same surgeon's site include men seeking correction of irregular forehead shape or hairline ridges and patients asking whether implants can add brow-bone projection [8].

Reviews of facial implant materials list autologous options (bone, cartilage, fat), titanium, silicone, porous polyethylene (MedPor), PEEK, PMMA and hydroxyapatite. They note that silicone has been associated with migration and bone resorption, porous polyethylene with one of the lowest reported infection rates and tissue incorporation, PEEK with mechanical strength, imaging compatibility and stable custom results, and PMMA with strength and common use in cranioplasty [4].

Cements are mixed in the operating room and molded on the bone while they set. PMMA is described by one surgeon as lower in cost per volume and at least as strong as bone, and as suited to larger augmentations; hydroxyapatite, which resembles the mineral phase of bone, is described as more natural and as bonding directly to bone, but costs more per gram and is reserved by that surgeon for modest augmentations [1]. Hydroxyapatite reviews describe it as biocompatible and osteoconductive but brittle and of low mechanical strength, potentially suited to non-load-bearing sites [5].

In the surgeon's published case example, a 35-year-old woman wanting a 5 to 6 mm increase in forehead and brow projection had hydroxyapatite cement placed through a coronal incision about 4 cm behind the hairline, with the forehead soft tissue lifted down, the cement shaped as it set and the scalp closed with dissolvable sutures [1]. Cement is generally positioned as suiting small-volume, smoothly contoured changes, and practitioners note it requires a longer scalp incision and a forehead flap [8][9].

Custom implants are designed on a computer from a CT scan, allowing the surgeon to preview shape and symmetry before surgery. The same surgeon argues that this gives more precision and a lower risk of revision for shape problems, that the implant can be placed through a smaller incision (he cites roughly 80 percent shorter) and that it can be designed to widen the forehead beyond the temporal lines [8][9][10]. He also describes using prefabricated MedPor implants and, more recently, custom implants, and says that screw fixation and perforation holes manage the empty space that can form under a custom implant [10].

These statements come from a practitioner's own clinical experience; no controlled study comparing cement with custom implants for forehead augmentation has been published, and reviews describe patient-specific implants as promising but needing further comparison [4][5].

Forehead work is a smaller topic than jaw and chin surgery in looksmaxxing forums, which are dominated by discussion of custom jaw, chin and wraparound implants, genioplasty, and surgeons such as Barry Eppley. Threads about implant materials debate silicone, Medpor, bioglass, PEEK, titanium and hydroxyapatite; one poster argued that silicone and Medpor carry a high infection risk and that Medpor ingrowth makes removal difficult, while replies urged consulting several surgeons [3]. Another thread on the same forum argues for hydroxyapatite over PEEK and titanium [12]. These are user opinions rather than research findings.

General risks of facial implant surgery include infection, swelling, asymmetry, displacement or exposure of the implant, and revision. In a systematic review of 12 studies (74 patients) on facial hydroxyapatite, eight studies reported no complications; the others described intraoperative implant fractures, one exposure requiring removal and, in orbital reconstruction, more serious problems, though none involved forehead augmentation specifically [5].

For cement specifically, the surgeon quoted above states that cement requires intraoperative shaping, can produce frontal bossing if placed too far forward, may fail to adhere or leave a visible edge if it extends past the temporal lines onto temporalis fascia, and has modestly high revision rates when large augmentation is wanted [10]. He also states that forehead implants are as safe as cements and carry no extra risk to the supraorbital nerves [10].

Complications in the related forehead surgery literature include frontal sinus problems. A 2024 cohort of 85 transfeminine patients undergoing forehead, hairline or brow feminization (mostly frontal bone setback, not augmentation) reported one mucocele and about 15 percent needing further surgery, mostly brow or scar revisions [7]. Facial feminization overviews list improper bone healing, fragment movement and cyst formation among cranioplasty risks that usually can be corrected with further surgery [6].

Forehead surgery for gender-affirming care developed from work by Douglas Ousterhout beginning in 1982, who defined feminine facial features from anthropological data and skull measurements [6]. For reduction of a prominent brow, surgeons burr the bone down and may smooth residual bulges with hydroxyapatite cement, or perform a cranioplasty in which the sinus wall is cut, thinned, reshaped and refixed [6].

A 2011 series of 21 male-to-female patients by Johannes Franz Hoenig used hydroxyapatite cement through a coronal approach to recontour the frontal bone after burring, with a median follow-up of 18 months; the author rated aesthetic results good to excellent in 15 patients and reported no complications [11]. These cases overlap with augmentation only in the use of cement for contouring.

No studies found that compare outcomes of forehead augmentation implants against cement. Related research includes the 2011 hydroxyapatite series and 2024 forehead feminization cohort described above [7][11], a 2024 systematic review of hydroxyapatite in facial implantology (12 studies, 74 patients, mostly level IV evidence, no comparisons with other materials) [5], and a 2024 review concluding that no facial implant material has been shown superior and that randomized trials are needed [4].

timeline.event: Douglas Ousterhout begins the facial feminization operations that standardise forehead recontouring techniques.[6]
Hoenig publishes a 21-patient series using hydroxyapatite cement to recontour the male-to-female forehead.[11]
Eppley publishes a case study of hydroxyapatite forehead and brow augmentation, describing PMMA, hydroxyapatite and custom implants.[1]
Reviews of facial implant materials and of facial hydroxyapatite conclude no material is established as superior.[4][5]
Khetpal and colleagues publish a scoping review and 85-patient cohort on forehead feminization.[7]

lore.intro: Forehead augmentation is discussed within the larger implant conversation on looksmax.org, where posters compare materials, designers and surgeons for jaw, chin and forehead work [3][12].

claims.claim: Custom CT-designed implants give a better forehead result than hand-shaped cement.
claims.believers: Surgeons who favour custom implants say they offer precise shape and symmetry, a smaller incision and fewer revisions for contour problems, [10][8].
claims.experts: These statements are practitioner opinion. Reviews describe patient-specific implants as promising but state that comparative trials against other materials are lacking [4][5].

claims.claim: Silicone and Medpor implants carry a high infection risk, so newer materials are preferable.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster argued that silicone and Medpor are infection-prone, that Medpor is hard to remove because of ingrowth, and floated bioglass, PEEK or titanium as alternatives [3].
claims.experts: A 2024 review reports silicone has been associated with migration and bone resorption, but also that porous polyethylene has one of the lowest reported infection rates; it finds no material definitively superior [4].

claims.claim: Hydroxyapatite is the best implant material.
claims.believers: A forum thread advocates hydroxyapatite over PEEK or titanium, and one surgeon describes it as natural and bone-bonding [12][1].
claims.experts: Reviews describe it as biocompatible and osteoconductive but brittle with limited long-term data and no comparative studies [5].

claims.claim: Forehead and brow implants endanger nerves or are riskier than other facial implants.
claims.believers: Some patients report being told by surgeons abroad that brow implants are dangerous because of nerves [10].
claims.experts: One implant surgeon states that forehead implants are as safe as cements and carry no extra risk to the supraorbital nerves; no controlled comparison is published [10].

claims.claim: Bone cement is fine for small, smooth changes but needs a long scalp incision.
claims.believers: Practitioners say cement suits small-volume contouring but requires a coronal incision and forehead flap [8][9].
claims.experts: A hydroxyapatite series using a coronal approach reported good to excellent results in most of 21 patients and no complications over about 18 months [11].

claims.claim: Large forehead augmentation with cement has a higher revision rate.
claims.believers: One surgeon describes modestly high revision rates for large cement augmentation, from bossing or visible edges [10].
claims.experts: Revision rates for cement augmentation have not been compared in controlled studies; hydroxyapatite reviews note possible underreporting of revisions [5].
